transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-20
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Jordan Miles (CTO - Nebula), Sasha Li (Head of ML - Nebula), Rafael Ortega (Platform Eng - Nebula)

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda — p95/p99 tail deep dive, streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs, KV cache behavior, batching strategies, and on-prem/VPC network hops. Priya will lead the tech part.
[00:20] Jordan Miles: Yeah thanks, we really want to understand our p99 spikes — they bite during peak and cause UI hitches. Currently we're seeing p95 around 120ms but p99 up to ~420ms on some endpoints.
[00:35] Priya Kapoor: Got it. Can you confirm: those numbers are client-side end-to-end or server-only? network included?
[00:45] Rafael Ortega: End-to-end from browser to our API gateway to the model endpoint, so includes network and a small proxy hop inside our VPC.
[01:05] Priya Kapoor: OK that helps. In our experience p99 often balloons because of three things: 1) cold KV cache misses or warmup, 2) variable batching windows causing long queueing, and 3) network tail hops — NAT, cross-AZ egress.
[01:25] Sasha Li: When you say KV cache, you mean the prefix/KV caching that Redwood runtime does? We have a lot of repeated system prompts and instruction prefixes.
[01:35] Priya Kapoor: Yes, the KV cache — sometimes folks call it the "KV cash" in notes — it's the per-session key-value attention cache. If you have repeated prefixes and we pin the session, p95/p99 drops a lot because less compute is needed. But cache misses can spike you.
[01:55] Alex Chen: Also want to call out streaming vs non-streaming. Streaming helps perceived latency for the user because first token arrives quicker, but p99 for total response completion can still be high if you block on finalization. We typically see streaming reduce p95 by ~30-50ms but p99 depends on how you measure it.
[02:20] Jordan Miles: Our UI measures time-to-first-byte and full-render. First byte is the priority but full render matters for batch results.
[02:35] Priya Kapoor: Right. A quick note on numbers — in our internal median workloads, p95 was ~90-130ms, p99 ~320-450ms depending on sequence length and model variant. On older GPU stacks without fused kernels p99 gets worse.
[03:00] Rafael Ortega: Our infra: AWS private subnet, cross-AZ for HA, internal NLB, and VPC endpoints. We're worried about additional hops if we move to Redwood Private in our VPC. Any guidance?
[03:15] Priya Kapoor: Network hops add deterministic latency and tail variance. Typical single AZ L7 hop is ~5-10ms, cross-AZ adds ~10-30ms variable. NAT/gateway and cross-account VPC peering can add 20-80ms in noisy cases. For p99-sensitive workloads we recommend colocating the model endpoint in the same AZ and use ENI-based routing where possible — that's the Dedicated/Private pattern.
[03:45] Jordan Miles: Makes sense. How about batching? We see latency increase when we increase batch sizes during peaks.
[03:55] Priya Kapoor: There's a tradeoff: batching increases throughput and lowers cost per token but can increase per-request latency because you wait for the batch window or token budget. We use adaptive batching and deadline-aware batching in the runtime; you can set per-route SLOs to bound wait windows. For strict p99 SLOs you might set a small max batch or use priority lanes.
[04:25] Sasha Li: Any quantitative guidance? e.g., batch window 5ms vs 20ms — typical p99 impact?
[04:35] Priya Kapoor: On typical NVMe/AMPere stacks, a 5–10ms batching window has minimal p95 increases but can still affect p99 by 30–60ms depending on queue behavior. 20ms windows will shift p99 by ~80–150ms in many cases. But large batches reduce compute time per token, so tail due to compute can reduce if the batch improves kernel throughput — it's workload dependent.
[05:05] Jordan Miles: You mentioned quantization. If we quantize to int8 or 4-bit, how does that affect tail latency and throughput?
[05:15] Priya Kapoor: Quantization reduces compute time — usually 15–40% improvement in per-token latency depending on model and kernel maturity. However, lower precision can change compute path and may increase variance if kernels are not well-optimized — sometimes p99 doesn't improve as much as median. We also watch for accuracy regressions; per-prompt evals are important.
[05:45] Rafael Ortega: We can run internal quality checks but need guidance on which prompts matter.
[05:50] Priya Kapoor: Send a representative prompt set — short and long tails — we have an eval harness. We'll run quantized candidate and produce delta reports (ROUGE, response differences) and latency distributions.
[06:05] Alex Chen: Quick interruption — Jordan, are you planning to host in your VPC (Redwood Private) or use Redwood Dedicated hosted?
[06:12] Jordan Miles: Prefer Private in our VPC for data residency and compliance, but we also want to keep the option to burst to hosted during spikes. Can Redwood do hybrid routing?
[06:25] Priya Kapoor: Yes, smart routing can failover to hosted variants; latency may change. For hybrid, be mindful of cross-network hops — bursting to hosted adds public egress unless we have private connectivity (Direct Connect, PrivateLink). That will impact p99.
[06:45] Sasha Li: Any comments on TLS termination and SSO that impact latency? Our security team insists on mutual TLS and SAML SSO at the edge.
[06:55] Priya Kapoor: TLS adds a small CPU cost at connection setup; reuse and keepalive minimize that. Mutual TLS and SAML shouldn't materially affect per-request token latency, as long as you have session caching and don't re-auth every request. Authz checks and heavy audit logging can add small tail variance if synchronous. We recommend batched/asynchronous audit ingestion for p99-sensitive paths.
[07:25] Rafael Ortega: Could you walk through a typical p95/p99 troubleshooting flow?
[07:30] Priya Kapoor: Sure. 1) validate measurement points (client vs server), 2) collect end-to-end traces and server-side histograms, 3) correlate with batch size and queue time, 4) check KV cache hit rate, 5) check cross-AZ network metrics, 6) test with quantized and unquantized models to separate compute vs network.
[07:55] Priya Kapoor: For traces we recommend capturing: request arrival, routing delay, batch entrance time, kernel start, kernel end, first token out, last token out, network egress. That helps attribute p99 to queueing vs compute vs network.
[08:15] Jordan Miles: We have observability but not token-level histograms. Can Redwood Console provide token-level breakdowns?
[08:22] Alex Chen: Yes, Redwood Console has per-token cost and latency breakdowns; we can enable token-level tracing for the POC. It's an add-on but useful for diagnosing tail.
[08:35] Sasha Li: We saw weird spikes when users sent many short chats concurrently. Is there a recommended pattern for small prompt routing?
[08:45] Priya Kapoor: For short requests, consider a micro-lane with tight batch windows and smaller max batch. Also prefix/KV caching helps if you have repeated system instructions. We also recommend aggressive early-init for sessions and warm caches during expected peak windows.
[09:10] Rafael Ortega: About KV cache eviction — how long do you keep per-session KV? We don't want memory blowup.
[09:18] Priya Kapoor: You can tune session TTLs and cache size by route. Default TTLs are modest (minutes) but for high-repeat workflows you can pin sessions longer. Redwood Dedicated/Private gives you more control over cache sizing and eviction policies.
[09:35] Jordan Miles: We'll likely need pinned sessions for agents to keep latency low.
[09:40] Priya Kapoor: Makes sense. We'll recommend a pilot config for agent workloads.
[09:45] Alex Chen: Can we talk about a recent case — Helix Tech — where p99 dropped after moving to single-AZ and enabling KV pinning?
[09:55] Priya Kapoor: Sure. Helix had p95 ~110ms and p99 ~480ms. After moving endpoints to same AZ as their API gateway and pinning KV per-session, p99 dropped to ~230ms. Streaming also improved perceived latency. They also adopted a small priority lane for interactive sessions.
[10:20] Sasha Li: That's promising. We need concrete numbers for our infra.
[10:25] Priya Kapoor: We'll run a controlled POC: 1) baseline unquantized in your VPC, same AZ configuration; 2) enable streaming and tuning; 3) run quantized candidate; 4) test hybrid burst path to hosted. We'll capture p50/p95/p99, queue times, kernel times, and network histograms.
[10:50] Jordan Miles: For the POC, can you run both streaming and non-streaming measurement? We need both metrics.
[10:55] Priya Kapoor: Absolutely. We'll provide per-route configs. Expect a typical timeline: onboarding + trace collection in ~3-5 days, initial analysis in 2 business days after traces, then a joint review.
[11:10] Rafael Ortega: What about security/compliance: SOC2 and KMS integration? Our CISO requires that logs remain in our account.
[11:20] Alex Chen: Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM integration and audit logs that can be forwarded to your SIEM. We'll surface the compliance docs and SOC2 report. We'll also provide an architecture note for on-prem and VPC-deployed audit retention.
[11:35] Priya Kapoor: On the POC, we'll request read-only access to perf metrics and agree on redwood-managed vs customer-managed logging.
[11:45] Sasha Li: Any gotchas with Direct Connect or PrivateLink for lower tail?
[11:50] Priya Kapoor: Direct Connect reduces variability by avoiding internet egress; PrivateLink keeps traffic within AWS backbone and is a good pattern for hybrid. Both reduce p99 variance. But if you still have cross-AZ routing on the other side, you'll see some tail.
[12:10] Jordan Miles: OK. Let's talk about measurements we'll share: we can provide 24 hours of request logs and traces. Anything else?
[12:20] Priya Kapoor: Also provide sample prompt set, user concurrency profile, and peak window patterns. If you can provide a small synthetic workload that replicates your client behavior (sequence lengths, token distribution), that's ideal.
[12:35] Alex Chen: We'll attach a benchmark spreadsheet link in the follow-up with columns for p50/p95/p99, queue time, kernel time, network e2e, and KV cache hit rate.
[12:50] Rafael Ortega: One more question — do you support per-route SLOs to automatically adjust batching?
[12:58] Priya Kapoor: Yes, route-level SLOs and autoscaling policies allow you to configure maximum batch windows and priority lanes. You can also set fallback routing to lower-cost models when latency budgets are exceeded.
[13:20] Jordan Miles: That fallback behavior — does it change the output quality? We need to be careful for customer-facing responses.
[13:28] Priya Kapoor: Fallback to a compatible variant may produce subtle quality differences. We recommend A/B testing and quality monitors; Redwood Optimize can alert on regressions tied to prompt sets.
[13:45] Sasha Li: Sounds good.
[13:50] Alex Chen: OK let's recap next steps. Priya will share the benchmark spreadsheet and a network trace checklist. Rafael will provide 24-hour sample traffic and prompt set. Alex will send POC commercial terms and an onboarding runbook. We'll schedule follow-up in 2 weeks.
[14:15] Jordan Miles: Great, thanks everyone.
[14:20] Priya Kapoor: Thanks — we'll get artifacts over.

Notes on transcript quality: auto transcription had a few errors ("KV cash" instead of KV cache; some names munged). Links referenced: Benchmark spreadsheet (Redwood internal link): https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/nebula-poc; Security docs: https://redwood.ai/security/nebula; POC runbook: drive link shared in chat.

End of meeting.
